title: Frith sets sights on NHS dental care beyond activity targets
html:
Dental minister James Frith outlined ambitions for a dental service focused on better oral health outcomes, as he promised further contract reform in England and spoke of restoring ‘some level of universal principle’ to NHS dentistry.

Addressing the General Dental Council’s Dental Leadership Network on 24 November, the Bury North MP said this year’s contract changes were only the beginning.

‘The 2026 reforms are a real step forward, but they are not the end of the journey. And in the long term, we are committed to improving access and reforming the dental contract as a key lever to achieve this goal.’

He said the emphasis on units of dental activity ‘has not aged well’ and argued for greater attention to the outcomes being commissioned.

‘I also want to get to a point where we can restore some level of universal principle, and there’ll be more to say on that in due course,’ he said.

Dentistry on the political agenda

Frith’s appearance and words offered an encouraging sign that dentistry might be gaining more attention within a government that had placed social care at the centre of its health agenda.

Frith joined the meeting after MPs had questioned him about dental access in the Commons, where he said ministers would ‘shortly’ publish their intentions for further reform. At the GDC event, he acknowledged how much dentistry mattered to voters.

‘Any MP just has to take one look at their inbox to know how much this matters to their constituents,’ he said, adding that dentistry was ‘one of the things that comes up most in the House of Commons tea room’.

However, Frith recently stopped short of confirming reform within this parliamentary term.

He also acknowledged a financial constraint. With the dental budget underspend reduced, further progress would need more money.

‘Anything further from here does require, by its very nature, additional funding,’ he said.

Crouch tests the promises

In closing remarks at the GDC event, British Dental Association chair Eddie Crouch brought the discussion back to the conditions needed to deliver care.

He questioned whether digital booking could solve poor access without funding alongside it. His leaky bucket analogy also challenged the emphasis on recruitment without addressing retention in NHS dentistry.

On the prospect of contract reform details arriving ‘shortly’, he was pointed.

‘I’ve been hearing shortly for a long while,’ he said.
